b: Chaosium has halted development of its crowdfunded Forbidden Stars remake, Old Ones Origins, after its designer Samuel Bailey was convicted of multiple child sex offences.

Bailey, 44, faces a potential life sentence after being found guilty of five counts of first-degree child rape and two counts of first-degree child molestation by a Washington State jury on November 12. He is due to be sentenced next month.

The conviction comes more than three years after criminal charges were first filed against Bailey, during which time he remained active in the board game industry – including demonstrating Old Ones Origins at Chaosium’s Gen Con booth in August this year. Court records show Bailey repeatedly sought and received permission to travel out of state while awaiting trial.
Samuel Bailey, left, demonstrating Old Ones Origins during Gen Con 2026

Chaosium told crowdfunding backers of the $770,000 Old Ones Origins campaign yesterday that it only learned of criminal proceedings against Bailey on Friday, November 13, which BoardGameWire understands occurred when a parent of one of the children alerted them via email.

The update to Gamefound backers said, “These are very serious crimes, and have significant legal implications on the Old Ones Origins board game, beyond the serious moral implications. We have stopped all development on this project.
“So please bear with us as we work with our legal counsel as to how move forward [sic]. We will be updating this as we get further confirmations.”

Chaosium has not yet provided answers to BoardGameWire’s questions about whether Bailey has already received payments for his design work, whether he remains entitled to royalties or other compensation following his conviction, or what contractual rights the company has to continue developing the game without him.

Company co-owner Michael O’Brien did confirm to BoardGameWire, “We just found about these criminal convictions and have stopped all development on this project. We are talking with legal counsel about next steps. We’ll have more to say in due course.”

The situation has thrown the future of the game into doubt for the campaign’s almost 3,000 backers – some of whom have demanded refunds and called for Bailey to be removed from the project so development can continue. Chaosium had initially planned to reopen the campaign for late pledges today.

The publisher said on Sunday that it had instructed Gamefound to halt scheduled Stretch Pay instalments, but warned that some payments might still be processed. Several backers subsequently reported that their payments had gone through as scheduled.
One parent of a child affected by the case, who cannot be named in order to protect the identity of the children, told BoardGameWire they believed Chaosium were also “in part a victim” of Bailey.

They said, “I believe Sam deceived them like he deceived most people in his life. He took advantage of his standing in the board game community knowing that most companies would not perform thorough background checks and see he had active charges for child rape and molestation.

“Sam had to get permission from the court to go to these conventions. Due to that I don’t 100% fault Chaosium for sending him all over the country. They were deceived and the courts approved him going, so he was able to keep up the deception.”

The parent added, “I believe it is immoral at this point knowing what they know to continue to receive funds for the game designed by Sam. I ask they do the right thing insofar as they can. I don’t want them to go bankrupt because of this nor do anything to try and make things right that would bankrupt them.
“However, they need to do everything in their power to remove Sam’s name and contributions from the game and any other products he collaborated with them on.”
They continued, “I know it is not common practice to perform background checks in this industry on independent contractors. Especially on established board game designers. That needs to change.

“Sam was out on bail for 3.5 years. These charges were publicly available. I want to see a real change. A great first starting point for the industry is thorough background checks on all people involved with the company.

“It does cost money to perform them, but it is a negligible cost at the end of the day given how small some of these companies are. They need to especially be done on people they plan on sending to conventions.
“I truly believe Chaosium would not be in this situation right now had they performed a thorough background check.”

Bailey’s conviction comes after months of Chaosium promoting his involvement in Old Ones Origins, highlighting his work as one of the designers of Fantasy Flight Games’ highly regarded 2015 Warhammer 40,000 strategy game Forbidden Stars – which was discontinued just two years later following the end of the publisher’s licensing agreement with Games Workshop.
Forbidden Stars || Photo Credit: Fantasy Flight Games

Bailey was one of three credited designers of Forbidden Stars, alongside Corey Konieczka and James Kniffen. The game was itself a reworking of Fantasy Flight’s 2007 release StarCraft: The Board Game, co-designed by Konieczka and Twilight Imperium creator Christian Petersen.

Chaosium formally unveiled Old Ones Origins the day before this year’s Gen Con, describing it as an “enhanced reimplementation” of Forbidden Stars set in the Cthulhu Mythos, retaining the original game’s asymmetric strategy gameplay while introducing new mechanics, factions and expansions.
Bailey personally demonstrated the game’s prototype at the convention, with Chaosium subsequently publishing photographs of him at its booth and promoting his role in the project.

That promotion continued throughout the Gamefound campaign, which launched on September 28, with the publisher releasing designer diaries, publicising interviews with Bailey and organising opportunities for backers to question him directly about the game’s development.

As recently as October 14, during the campaign’s final 24 hours, Chaosium published an extensive collection of questions and answers attributed to Bailey, covering his approach to redesigning Forbidden Stars, gameplay balance, playtesting and potential future expansions.
Chaosium had been targeting January 2028 for delivery of English-language copies of Old Ones Origins, with translated editions expected to follow in July that year.

Bailey worked in board game retail before joining Fantasy Flight Games in 2013, working on expansions for Talisman, Elder Sign and Mansions of Madness before the release of Forbidden Stars two years later.
He left FFG in 2016 to become a freelance board game designer, but did not release a published design after FFG until Lawyer Up!, his co-design with Mike Gnade, in 2021.
Bailey was involved in a public dispute with Root publisher Leder Games in 2018, after the publisher cancelled development of his asymmetric science-fiction strategy game Deep: Enemy Frontier.
He accused Leder of breaching its contract and alleged that Root, the publisher’s forthcoming game designed by Cole Wehrle, had borrowed elements of his work.

Wehrle strongly rejected the allegations, saying that “no mechanical element of Root was taken from Deep. None.” He acknowledged having played and worked on elements of Bailey’s game, but said he had deliberately taken Root in a different direction to avoid overlapping with it, drawing on geopolitics and historical wargames rather than Deep’s science-fiction and 4X influences.

He accused Bailey at the time of misrepresenting the circumstances of Deep’s cancellation, but declined to detail the problems encountered during development, saying he did not want to damage Bailey’s prospects of finding another publisher.
BoardGameWire has approached Chaosium with multiple questions about the situation with Bailey, and will update this article or run a follow-up piece if they respond with more detail.
